questions.prompt: In Claude's guide, which version of a safety criterion is the good one?

options.text: Under 0.1% of outputs out of 10,000 trials flagged for toxicity by the content filter
options.explanation: Right. This is the guide's own example of a measurable safety criterion.

options.text: Outputs that are safe enough that a reasonable person would not complain about them
options.explanation: This depends on who complains. The guide calls for a measurable criterion.

options.text: Safe outputs, as judged by the team once it feels confident about the release date
options.explanation: "Safe outputs" is the guide's bad example. A feeling of confidence is not a measure.

questions.prompt: OpenAI's evaluation guide says to "log everything". Why?

options.text: So the logs can replace the test set as soon as they grow large enough to look complete
options.explanation: Logs feed the test set. They do not replace choosing and grading cases.

options.text: So you can mine them for good eval cases while you build and test the product
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI docs say to log as you develop, so you can mine the logs for good eval cases.

options.text: So reviewers can skip reading outputs and trust the scores that are stored in the log
options.explanation: The guide asks for human feedback to calibrate automated scores. It does not say to skip reading.

questions.prompt: What do the OpenAI docs name as a "vibe-based eval"?

options.text: Judging every image by its colours and mood, as many creative teams often do
options.explanation: The anti-pattern is about the test method, not about colours or mood.

options.text: Running many small evals at once so that no one score counts for very much at all
options.explanation: The guide does not describe that. Running evals often is its advice.

options.text: Using "it seems like it's working" as the test, or waiting for launch to build evals
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI docs list both as the anti-pattern.
